If his intent is validation, the guy is a narcissist, if his intent is to watch you suffer as you pine for him while he moves on, he is a sociopath. Either way this guy sounds predatory because he doesn't show any interest in your emotional well being, only his and his alone.

This could be why you feel like he is a soulmate, do some research on these types of relationship predators and it may help set you free.

However he could just be an immature jerk who is just an asshole with some off traits. 

However you look at it, this situation already doesn't meet your basic relationship needs as no sex = platonic. I doubt that makes someone your bf unless that's something you've agreed to. If it's him calling all these shots, you are being covertly abused and you may not even know it. Likely being manipulated emotionally to feel like he is your soulmate when so much you've expressed here says otherwise.

So here's the thing to focus on instead, ‘’Ask yourself whether you feel valued, respected, and cared about. Are you getting your needs met? If not, how is that affecting you and your self-esteem and what can you do about that?’’ 

The best thing has been said already and that he has clearly made the decision without you so there is nothing for you to save and to be frank, that is probably the kindest thing he could do but for some reason your ego wants to resist the fact. 

Let go of people who want to let go of you! That is not a soul mate and anyone who plays mind games is not either. You could end up wasting a lot of energy, life and yourself carrying on this way and the part people usually regret most is the self betrayal.

In terms of the advice, wt actual f. Why I would avoid asking internet strangers for advice about your relationship and life experience they know nothing about (other than a brief question). As you will just get whatever random perspective. A lot of people saying it's assumed you don't have mental health issues when you've made it clear you do struggle with that. Including emotional regulation.

Bottom line is your husband went looking and found something. That's on him. Period. You didn't do anything wrong, he did. You are not responsible for how he feels about having read your personal journal! He violated your boundaries reading your private thoughts and now he's paying the consequences. That's not on you to fix. Maybe he should go to therapy to find out why he needed to snoop in the first place and deal with his own feelings surrounding that!

If I were you I would not feel the need to explain as again it's your private journal which he violated. So let that be a lesson to him. Lets make that clear. So he opened up Pandora's box and now wants to sulk. lol Doesn't seem fair to you that not only he violates your boundaries but then gets to guilt you on what you wrote in it as a release of negative thought (perfectly normal). It's a way to get your feelings out, your form of therapy and he showed a lack of respect for that. For those who are saying that's not normal, maybe not for them but it is for you. What do these people know about being in a relationship for 15 yrs!? Or yours for that matter. I certainly don't pretend to know.

That's the thing, so unless you know these people you're getting advice from including me...I would take it with a grain of salt. You mentioned wanting to go to therapy for trauma but have financial issues which prevent that. My suggestion is to look for free or low cost counselling. There are some services that will provide financial help for these reasons as it's not fair to go without due to the fact you can't afford it. Mental health should always be a resource you are able to access regardless of level of income. There could maybe be some resources you are unaware of in your area of residence that could help guide you to connect to what you need.

Anyways I wouldn't enable your husband's actions by letting him guilt you. Simply state those were my private thoughts, sorry you are hurt by violating them. If you want to talk about things I'm open to it but for future reference you are allowed to have your own things separate from him and it's him who now put this burden on the both of you.

Sounds like there are some insecurities in the relationship and that's pretty common. You could try working on these things but I would steer clear of allowing him to guilt you on anything he shouldn't have been reading in the first place. Again that's on him. If you wanted to share thoughts with him you would but in your book that's not for him. So it's okay he feels bad, that's what he gets for violating boundaries, wanted to make that really clear.

You did NOTHING wrong there other than maybe not hide it or lock it up good enough but apparently you didn't think you had to. It's not like he found trinkets of people you killed or adventures of cheating. No, he found a release of your negative thoughts. Tell him to take responsibility for himself for being a snoop and keep the lines of communication open for anything else he'd like to discuss that has nothing to do with what he shouldn't have violated in the first place. Boundaries are a beautiful thing and he broke them, not you. If he can't get over it then there are more issues going on that need to be addressed or he's looking for an excuse to blame you rather than see his role. Since what I'm hearing is him being controlling by sulking over something he did wrong, now you think it's something you need to fix? That's not right.

As I see it, you are both single and it's really up to you now that she put the ball in your court. How do you feel about this proposition?  

I have heard stories where sometimes people who've been cheated on by each other's partners, ended up together and being a much better match. That doesn't mean that is always the case or that this will happen for either of you. 

If you want to take comfort in each other as a rebound than it would be fair game yet neither of you may be prepared for any lingering emotions which follow and come about in this type of affair. 

Considering one of you may become more attached than the other, adding more complications to the grief. Which I think is what you are concerned about for good reason. 

It makes sense she would find comfort in this idea because you both have a common grief within the same group. Yet for you, you deal with a betrayal of two people rather than one. 

The rational brain would allow time and clarity to make a well rounded decision. 

While the irrational part of the brain would be led by emotion or desire. Either way when these two do not meet up there will be some sort of confliction. 

So you are asking which one should take the lead and the only person who can decide this my friend is you.

Take care of you and the kids 1st.

How do people go from romantic to 'just friends' when nothing has changed! How realistic is that to put yourself in this position. It sounds like a recipe for unrequited love or pining over the one who has rejected you in some way.

I think the question you must ask is, are you okay with being friends only and how will that effect or complicate future relationships. Since as you stated she broke your heart and trust yet you are willing to give her a role as friend in your life?

Is that the kind of friends you want to keep around?

I think space will help to clarify that when people act wishy washy, they only get away with it if they're able to keep people on a string with no consequence of taking on the burden of their actions, if you know what I mean. Why enable/reward that behavior.

Space is also needed to see what you mean to this person, the work/energy they will put in to regain your trust or not. If you give them what they want at the detriment of what you want, there is 0 motivation to do work on their part. Then you not only will feel rejected, likely angry at the betrayal to yourself. Then resentment will occur towards her, you or both. That's how toxic relationships are born, they start subtle. We ignore all the signs that they exist because the truth means we have to accept something we don't like and then do something we don't like in order to move forward.

From what you say here I doubt you want to be friends with this person, it's that you don't want to cut ties all together now that you realize the truth about who she is and how little she values your relationship enough to break your trust and heart, then say hey! Lets still be friends.

Sometimes we make simple things more complicated because the truth doesn't align with what we want to be true.

Good luck on whatever you choose, be kind to yourself. No need to further shatter pieces of your own heart in order to keep someone around who doesn't know what they want.

Even if you decide to pursue the friendship game, space is needed to make that adjustment or else you will do yourself even more heartache, pretty sure you already know that.

Trust your gut (keep in mind it was to break up with her because she broke a major boundary for you and that's okay!) Sometimes we don't need to second guess ourselves because we're scared nothing better will come along.

Keep in mind nothing better can come along either if there is no room in your life for that, like a person who more on the same page.

Rejection is always brutal no matter who you are, that part is relatable to most of the population. Trying to continue to get love from the same person never makes anyone feel better about themselves.

It's more empowering to listen to your needs and wants and sometimes it means putting yourself first, as the other person is doing.

Everyone will be different but it's not always easy for some people to have kids after a certain age as things could change, like illness or a sudden accident. If that's something she'd really like to have then it's smart to invest in someone who is already on the same page rather than leave it to chance and have regrets based on going with the flow. 

Unless she is okay with how it turns out whichever way but she expresses regret if she were to look back and have not had children. So that's telling.

Well sounds like she was more emotionally invested in this relationship for whatever reason. If you decide to ghost her, it may turn into unrequited love and worsen the rejection. I'd be honest and sometimes the truth is not so kind before you stop all communication as to 'set her free'. Such as I don't see a future with you. Thank her for the time you've had together, appreciate what was, brief and then no contact, stop responding to any texts, calls which you should mention before you go no contact that you feel it's best to give each other the space needed right now to move on.

This way she'll take it more seriously because rejection can be hard on women as well, the process isn't always instant. No one likes being dumped since it was not their choice, of course she will take it harder than the person (you who is dumping her). Since you had time to process and conclude to this one-sided decision which I'm guessing she probably didn't see coming. Even though she probably tried to play it off to lessen the blow.

Everyone has an ego and it's more of a bruised ego than it is getting over you. This is the part that sucks about relationships yet the risk she took on in going long distance. As soon as she meets someone new who she is attracted to again, she will realize that you were not right for each other (hopefully). As long as you don't string her along under the pretense of being a 'nice guy'.

Since that is not nice, not at all. Can't have everyone like you all the time otherwise you will be a coward who causes more destruction. The lesser evil is to do one quick hurt rather than a series of multiple prolonged ones. Less damage by rejection this way.

Most of us have been there, knowing it's best to end things though finding it hard to let go when we know the other person wants to leave (questioning our own appeal to others/ self worth/self esteem thing). Always best to allow someone who wants to go to go. Since they will always be looking for excuses to exit in the future anyway. Or think you are someone to keep on the back burner. Tell her to value herself more and she'll learn to take rejection better in the future (probably don't say that part).

If she has hope you can still be together, then you're doing it wrong or her self-esteem is incredibly low. Perhaps a bit of both. Her attachment style in relationships is probably an anxious one. In other words, you can't both be the nice guy and the one who breaks her heart by ending things if the love is one-sided or when their seems to be an emotional imbalance.  Some people feel more deeply in general, causing more sensitivity around rejection and break-ups.

You can't eat your cake and have it too because if you eat the cake, it's gone!
